summary: Tackles differences between sites' tables of Host names and network addresses and proposes how to resolve them. It is one of several related early notes on providing host names on-line, alongside RFCs 608, 623, 625 and 627.

plainLanguage.summary: Each computer kept its own address book and the books disagreed. This note starts fixing that with a shared one.

subtitle: A proposal for one official, machine-readable host name file kept on-line by the NIC.

tldr.problem: Every site kept its own slightly different and out-of-date list mapping host names to host addresses.
tldr.mechanism: The NIC would keep one on-line ASCII file of entries, each with a host name and address and optional attribute=value pairs such as NICKNAMES, FTP-BYTE-SIZES and ECHOING.
tldr.outcome: The file is meant as a simple extra source of information, not a replacement for option negotiation or other ways hosts learn each other's properties.

today: The unit metadata lists the status as Unknown and shows no later RFC replacing it. The text is a proposal and does not say whether it was adopted.

sections.title: Why a Central Host List
sections.content:
L. Peter Deutsch notes that an official list of host names now exists, so the absurd situation of each site keeping a different, generally out-of-date list should end. He observes that the TENEX sites he uses (SRI-ARC, BBN-TENEX, USC-ISI and PARC-MAXC) each have a slightly different mapping, none complete.

The NIC is responsible for the official list, so he proposes it maintain an on-line file, accessible to anyone, in an easily machine-readable form. He rules out an NLS structured file, since there are no facilities to access those from the network.
sections.plainLanguage: Each school kept its own class list and the lists did not match. He asks the office to keep one list everyone can read.

sections.title: What the File Holds
sections.content:
Each entry has the official host name and host address. Optional extras are protocol options, including the preferred FTP byte size and the preferred TELNET duplex mode, and the host's function (user, server, TIP and so on), which could help NCPs decide whether to poll a host or collect statistics.

Because the file is generated centrally but used widely, it should be easy to interrogate even at the expense of ease of construction. He suggests an ASCII text file with the structure of a property list of attribute and value pairs.
sections.plainLanguage: The list gives each computer's name and number, plus a few extra notes about how it likes to be talked to.

sections.title: The Proposed Syntax
sections.content:
An entry is a basic part, host-name , host-address, followed by attribute items of the form attribute-name = attribute-value, each ending in an end-of-line, with a blank line after the entry. Names follow RFC 597: letters, digits, hyphens and parentheses. The address is decimal, relative to its own network. He favors carriage-return followed by line-feed as end-of-line.

Suggested attributes are NICKNAMES (acceptable alternatives), FTP-BYTE-SIZES (the first being cheapest to compute, such as 36 for PDP-10s and 32 for 360s) and ECHOING (L or R for local or remote echo). No attribute is required.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line is like "name = value", for example "nickname = something", so a program can find what it wants without guessing.

sections.title: Limits and Caveats
sections.content: The file is meant not to replace option negotiation or word-of-mouth, only to give another simple, uniform source. The author admits it is a specific solution to a specific problem, but says the problem had irked him for well over a year and nobody seemed interested in a more general one. He asks that anyone who can do the same job through the Datacomputer write an RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a quick fix, not a grand plan, and he says so honestly.
